warmup.q: record Masked(String card) overrides its accessor so that card() returns "****1111" for the card 4111111111111111. What does toString() return?
options: Nothing: it doesn't compile, because record accessors can't be overridden
Masked@1b6d3586, because overriding an accessor turns off the generated toString
warmup.why: The generated toString, equals and hashCode read the private field directly, not the accessor, so the full number reaches the log. Overriding an accessor is legal as long as the return type matches. To hide a component, override toString itself, as the lab does.

sections.h: A record is its components, and javac writes the rest
sections.html:
Write one line:

Java
public record Money(long minor, String currency) {}
Kotlin
data class Money(val minor: Long, val currency: String)

From that line javac generates a private final field per component, a public accessor per component (minor() and currency(), with no get prefix), a canonical constructor that takes the components in order, and equals, hashCode and toString. The class is final and extends java.lang.Record. Records have been final since JDK 16 (JEP 395), so everything in this lesson works on the JDK 21 the labs compile for.

The Record Javadoc calls a record "a shallowly immutable, transparent carrier for a fixed set of values". Each part of that phrase is a rule you will run into. The component list is fixed: you can't add instance fields, and private int cache; in the body fails with field declaration must be static. Static fields, methods and nested types are fine. Transparent means the state is the API. Every component gets a public accessor, and equals and toString use every component. A record can implement interfaces but can't extend a class, because it already extends Record. And shallowly immutable means the fields are final while the objects they point to may not be. Section 3 is about that.

The generated methods are not what you would write by hand. javap shows that equals, hashCode and toString are each a single invokedynamic call to java.lang.runtime.ObjectMethods.bootstrap. javac passes it the component names as one string (minor;currency) and a direct getter for each private field. At run time the JDK builds the method bodies from that list, which is why the Javadoc says the exact hashCode algorithm and toString format may change: never parse a record's toString. kotlinc does it the older way and writes equals and hashCode out as ordinary bytecode in your class.

A record is still an ordinary object with its own identity. new Point(3, 4) == new Point(3, 4) is false, and synchronized on a record compiles and runs. Objects without identity are what Project Valhalla adds, as a preview feature scheduled for JDK 28. Lesson 4 of this track covers where that stands.

try.title: Look inside a record
steps: Run RecordAnatomy (or its Kotlin twin) with the command below. Predict the == line before you look.
From labs/, print the bytecode of the nested record: javap -p -c 'modernjava/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/modernjava/l01/demo/RecordAnatomy$Point.class'. Find the three invokedynamic lines.
Run javap -v on the same file and scroll to BootstrapMethods. Then run javap -p modernjava/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/modernjava/l01/demo/Point.class and compare what kotlinc generated.

code.title: RecordAnatomy.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo; import java.util.Arrays; /** What javac gives a one-line record, seen from the outside. */ public class RecordAnatomy { record Point(int x, int y) {} public static void main(String[] args) { Point a = new Point(3, 4); Point b = new Point(3, 4); System.out.println("toString: " + a); System.out.println("accessors: x()=" + a.x() + " y()=" + a.y()); System.out.println("equals: " + a.equals(b) + ", same hashCode: " + (a.hashCode() == b.hashCode())); System.out.println("==: " + (a == b) + " (two objects, each with its own identity)"); System.out.println("isRecord: " + Point.class.isRecord()); System.out.println("components: " + Arrays.toString(Point.class.getRecordComponents())); System.out.println("superclass: " + Point.class.getSuperclass().getName()); synchronized (a) { // compiles and runs: a record is an ordinary identity object System.out.println("locked on a record"); } } }

alt.title: RecordAnatomy.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo // a plain data class: Kotlin generates equals, hashCode, toString, componentN and copy data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int) // the same data class, also emitted as a real JVM record (java.lang.Record subclass) @JvmRecord data class RecordPoint(val x: Int, val y: Int) /** What kotlinc gives a one-line data class, seen from the outside. */ fun main() { val a = Point(3, 4) val b = Point(3, 4) println("toString: $a") println("properties: x=${a.x} y=${a.y}") println("equals: ${a == b}, same hashCode: ${a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()}") println("===: ${a === b} (two objects, each with its own identity)") println("isRecord: ${Point::class.java.isRecord} for the data class, ${RecordPoint::class.java.isRecord} with @JvmRecord") println("components: ${RecordPoint::class.java.recordComponents.contentToString()}") println("superclass: ${RecordPoint::class.java.superclass.name}") println("copy: ${a.copy(y = 10)}") synchronized(a) { // compiles and runs: a data class instance is an ordinary identity object println("locked on a data class") } }

try.expect: The demo prints Point[x=3, y=4], equals: true, ==: false, isRecord: true and the components [int x, int y]. The Kotlin twin prints isRecord: false for the plain data class and true for the @JvmRecord one. Under BootstrapMethods there is one ObjectMethods.bootstrap entry whose arguments are the class, x;y, and two REF_getField handles on the private fields. The Kotlin class has getX(), component1(), copy(int, int) and copy$default(...) instead.

sections.h: The compact constructor is the only way in
sections.html:
A record has exactly one canonical constructor: the one whose parameters match the components. Every other constructor must call it first, and so does every static factory, every wither, and Java deserialization. That makes it the one place for validation and normalization. Write it in the compact form, with no parameter list:

Java
public record Money(long minor, String currency) {
    public Money {
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency");
        if (minor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount: " + minor);
        currency = currency.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT);    // reassign the parameter
    }                                                    // javac assigns the fields here

    public Money(long minor) { this(minor, "EUR"); }     // must delegate first
}
Kotlin
data class Money(val minor: Long, val currency: String) {
    init {
        require(minor >= 0) { "negative amount: $minor" }
        require(currency == currency.uppercase()) { "currency must be upper case: $currency" }
    }

    constructor(minor: Long) : this(minor, "EUR")        // must delegate first
}

In the compact form the parameters are ordinary local variables. You can reassign them, and javac copies their final values into the fields after your code runs. You can't touch the fields yourself: this.minor = minor; fails with cannot assign a value to final variable minor. A non-canonical constructor that doesn't start with this(...) fails on JDK 21 with constructor is not canonical, so its first statement must invoke another constructor of class Money. JDK 25 made flexible constructor bodies final, so there you may run plain statements, such as parsing "12.50 EUR", before the this(...) call.

The Kotlin version shows a real difference. init runs on every construction, and copy() runs it too. But a data class can't change a constructor parameter before it becomes a property. It can reject "eur", but it can't turn it into "EUR". Normalizing moves into a factory function, and the public constructor still accepts the raw value.

Deserialization is where the canonical constructor pays off. The Record Javadoc says the canonical constructor is invoked during deserialization, and that readObject and writeObject are ignored for records. An ordinary class needs a hand-written readObject to recheck its invariants, and most classes don't have one. A record gets the check for free. A Kotlin data class does not: Java deserialization never runs its init block, unless you mark the class @JvmRecord so it compiles to a real record. The Try it below tampers with a byte stream to show both.

try.title: Go through every door
steps: Run CompactConstructorDemo. Read the last line of output before you read the code that produced it.
Run the Kotlin twin, CompactConstructorDemoKt. Which tampered range got through?
In the Java demo, add this.minor = minor; inside the compact constructor of Money and run again. Read the compiler error, then undo the change.
If you have JDK 25, run java preview/FlexibleConstructor.java from labs/modernjava. Then run the same file with JDK 21 and read the two errors.

code.title: CompactConstructorDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo; import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream; import java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream; import java.io.ObjectInputStream; import java.io.ObjectOutputStream; import java.io.Serializable; import java.util.Locale; import java.util.Objects; /** Every way of making a record goes through its canonical constructor, even deserialization. */ public class CompactConstructorDemo { record Money(long minor, String currency) { Money { // compact canonical constructor Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency"); if (minor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount: " + minor); currency = currency.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT); // reassign the parameter } // fields are assigned here Money(long minor) { this(minor, "EUR"); } // non-canonical: must delegate static Money ofMajor(long major, String ccy) { // a factory: still goes through it return new Money(Math.multiplyExact(major, 100), ccy); } } record Range(int lo, int hi) implements Serializable { Range { if (lo > hi) throw new IllegalArgumentException("lo > hi: " + lo + " > " + hi); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println(new Money(1250, "eur")); System.out.println(new Money(5)); System.out.println(Money.ofMajor(3, "usd")); try { new Money(-1, "EUR"); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("IAE: " + e.getMessage()); } try { new Money(1, null); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("NPE: " + e.getMessage()); } // serialize a valid Range, then swap its two int fields in the byte stream byte[] bytes = serialize(new Range(1, 5)); swapLastTwoInts(bytes); try (var in = new ObjectInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes))) { System.out.println("tampered stream gave: " + in.readObject()); } catch (java.io.InvalidObjectException e) { System.out.println("tampered stream rejected: " + e.getMessage()); } } static byte[] serialize(Object o) throws Exception { var buf = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); try (var out = new ObjectOutputStream(buf)) { out.writeObject(o); } return buf.toByteArray(); } // the stream ends with the int fields (hi, then lo); swapping them turns (1, 5) into (5, 1) static void swapLastTwoInts(byte[] b) { int n = b.length; for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { byte t = b[n - 8 + i]; b[n - 8 + i] = b[n - 4 + i]; b[n - 4 + i] = t; } } }

alt.title: CompactConstructorDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream import java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream import java.io.InvalidObjectException import java.io.ObjectInputStream import java.io.ObjectOutputStream import java.io.Serializable // Kotlin's init block is the compact constructor's twin: it runs on every construction. // Kotlin can't reassign a constructor parameter, so normalizing happens in a factory instead. data class Amount(val minor: Long, val currency: String) { init { require(minor >= 0) { "negative amount: $minor" } require(currency == currency.uppercase()) { "currency must be upper case: $currency" } } constructor(minor: Long) : this(minor, "EUR") // secondary: must delegate companion object { fun of(minor: Long, ccy: String) = Amount(minor, ccy.uppercase()) // normalize, then construct fun ofMajor(major: Long, ccy: String) = of(Math.multiplyExact(major, 100L), ccy) } } data class RangeK(val lo: Int, val hi: Int) : Serializable { init { require(lo <= hi) { "lo > hi: $lo > $hi" } } } @JvmRecord // a real JVM record data class RangeR(val lo: Int, val hi: Int) : Serializable { init { require(lo <= hi) { "lo > hi: $lo > $hi" } } } /** Every way of making a data class runs init... except Java deserialization of a plain data class. */ fun main() { println(Amount.of(1250, "eur")) println(Amount(5)) println(Amount.ofMajor(3, "usd")) try { Amount(-1, "EUR") } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("IAE: ${e.message}") } for (range in listOf<Any>(RangeK(1, 5), RangeR(1, 5))) { val bytes = serialize(range) swapLastTwoInts(bytes) try { val back = ObjectInputStream(ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)).use { it.readObject() } println("tampered stream gave: $back") } catch (e: InvalidObjectException) { println("tampered stream rejected: ${e.message}") } } } private fun serialize(o: Any): ByteArray { val buf = ByteArrayOutputStream() ObjectOutputStream(buf).use { it.writeObject(o) } return buf.toByteArray() } // the stream ends with the int fields (hi, then lo); swapping them turns (1, 5) into (5, 1) private fun swapLastTwoInts(b: ByteArray) { val n = b.size for (i in 0 until 4) { val t = b[n - 8 + i] b[n - 8 + i] = b[n - 4 + i] b[n - 4 + i] = t } }

try.expect: The Java demo prints Money[minor=1250, currency=EUR], Money[minor=5, currency=EUR], Money[minor=300, currency=USD], IAE: negative amount: -1, NPE: currency and finally tampered stream rejected: lo > hi: 5 > 1: deserialization called the compact constructor, it threw, and ObjectInputStream wrapped that in an InvalidObjectException. The Kotlin twin prints tampered stream gave: RangeK(lo=5, hi=1) for the plain data class, an object its own init forbids, and rejects the @JvmRecord one. The field assignment fails with cannot assign a value to final variable minor. On JDK 25 the preview file parses 12.50 eur into Money[minor=1250, currency=EUR]; JDK 21 rejects it.

sections.h: Equality and immutability go one level deep
sections.html:
equals on a record returns true when the other object is the same record class and every component is equal. For a reference component that means Objects.equals. For a primitive it means the wrapper's compare returns 0, which has two surprises for a double. A record holding NaN equals another one holding NaN, though NaN == NaN is false. And 0.0 and -0.0 are not equal, though 0.0 == -0.0 is true. Kotlin data classes behave the same way. Keep money in a long of minor units and neither will bite you.

Arrays are worse. An int[] component compares by reference, so two records with equal arrays are not equal, and toString prints something like [I@1b6d3586. Use a List.

A List component brings the real trap. The record holds a reference to whatever list the caller passed in, and if the caller keeps changing that list, the record changes too:

Java
record Batch(String id, List<String> paymentIds) {}

var ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay_1", "pay_2"));
var batch = new Batch("b-7", ids);
var sent = new HashSet<>(Set.of(batch));
ids.add("pay_3");
sent.contains(batch);              // false: the hashCode changed under the set
Kotlin
data class Batch(val id: String, val paymentIds: List<String>)

val ids = mutableListOf("pay_1", "pay_2")
val batch = Batch("b-7", ids)
val sent = hashSetOf(batch)
ids += "pay_3"
batch in sent                      // false: the hashCode changed under the set

The batch is still in the set. The set just looks for it in the wrong bucket. The fix is one line in the compact constructor: paymentIds = List.copyOf(paymentIds);. It makes an unmodifiable copy, and it throws NullPointerException for a null element. That is what you want for domain data, and a surprise for JSON lists that contain nulls. Kotlin's List<String> is a read-only view, not an immutable list, so a data class needs the same copy, made in a factory. Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal in the concurrency track made the same point about sharing between threads. Here the cost is a lost key, even on one thread.

The last trap looks like a fix. To keep a card number out of the logs, someone overrides the accessor so card() returns ****1111. The logs don't change. The generated toString reads the field directly (that is what the getters in the bootstrap arguments are), so it still prints the full number. The override also breaks the record contract that new Masked(m.card()) equals m. Record patterns, which lesson 3 covers, do call the accessor, so different parts of your code now see different data. To hide a component, override toString, or keep the secret out of any record that gets logged.

try.title: Lose a key, leak a card
steps: Give Batch a compact constructor that copies its list, as SafeBatch does. Run it again.
Run the Kotlin twin and look at the copy shares list line. Did copy() copy the list?

code.title: ShallowDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; /** Equality, hashCode and toString are only as deep as the components. */ public class ShallowDemo { record Batch(String id, List<String> paymentIds) {} record SafeBatch(String id, List<String> paymentIds) { SafeBatch { paymentIds = List.copyOf(paymentIds); } // unmodifiable copy } record Masked(String card) { @Override public String card() { return "****" + card.substring(card.length() - 4); } } record Rate(double value) {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay_1", "pay_2")); Batch batch = new Batch("b-7", ids); Set<Batch> sent = new HashSet<>(Set.of(batch)); int before = batch.hashCode(); ids.add("pay_3"); // someone reuses their list System.out.println("batch now: " + batch); System.out.println("hashCode changed: " + (before != batch.hashCode())); System.out.println("sent.contains: " + sent.contains(batch)); List<String> ids2 = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay_1", "pay_2")); SafeBatch safe = new SafeBatch("b-8", ids2); ids2.add("pay_3"); System.out.println("safe batch: " + safe); Masked m = new Masked("4111111111111111"); System.out.println("accessor: " + m.card()); System.out.println("toString: " + m); System.out.println("copy equals orig: " + new Masked(m.card()).equals(m)); System.out.println("NaN record equals: " + new Rate(Double.NaN).equals(new Rate(Double.NaN)) + " (but NaN == NaN is " + (Double.NaN == Double.NaN) + ")"); System.out.println("0.0 vs -0.0 equals: " + new Rate(0.0).equals(new Rate(-0.0)) + " (but 0.0 == -0.0 is " + (0.0 == -0.0) + ")"); } }

alt.title: ShallowDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo // List<String> is a read-only view in Kotlin, not an immutable list: the caller may still hold a MutableList data class Batch(val id: String, val paymentIds: List<String>) // Kotlin can't reassign a constructor parameter, so the defensive copy goes in a factory data class SafeBatch(val id: String, val paymentIds: List<String>) { companion object { fun of(id: String, paymentIds: List<String>) = SafeBatch(id, java.util.List.copyOf(paymentIds)) } } data class Rate(val value: Double) /** Equality, hashCode and toString are only as deep as the properties. */ fun main() { val ids = mutableListOf("pay_1", "pay_2") val batch = Batch("b-7", ids) val sent = hashSetOf(batch) val before = batch.hashCode() ids += "pay_3" // someone reuses their list println("batch now: $batch") println("hashCode changed: ${before != batch.hashCode()}") println("sent.contains: ${batch in sent}") val copy = batch.copy(id = "b-9") // copy() is shallow too ids += "pay_4" println("copy shares list: $copy") val ids2 = mutableListOf("pay_1", "pay_2") val safe = SafeBatch.of("b-8", ids2) ids2 += "pay_3" println("safe batch: $safe") println("NaN data class ==: ${Rate(Double.NaN) == Rate(Double.NaN)} (but NaN == NaN is ${Double.NaN == Double.NaN})") println("0.0 vs -0.0 ==: ${Rate(0.0) == Rate(-0.0)} (but 0.0 == -0.0 is ${0.0 == -0.0})") }

try.expect: hashCode changed: true and sent.contains: false. After your fix the batch keeps two ids and the set finds it. The masked record prints accessor: ****1111 but toString: Masked[card=4111111111111111], and copy equals orig: false. The NaN records are equal and the 0.0/-0.0 ones are not. In Kotlin, the copy shows pay_4, which was added after the copy was made: copy() copies references, not the objects behind them.

sections.h: Records, data classes and the missing copy()
sections.html:
Kotlin engineers reach for copy() first and find Java has none. A record that needs "the same refund with a smaller amount" gets a hand-written wither:

Java
record Refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor, List<String> reasons) {
    Refund withAmount(long newAmount) {
        return new Refund(paymentId, newAmount, reasons);   // through the canonical constructor
    }
}
Kotlin
data class Refund(val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long, val reasons: List<String>)

val part = full.copy(amountMinor = 2_000)                  // generated, and it runs init

Both go through validation, which is the point: there is no path to an invalid Refund. The cost on the Java side is typing, and it grows with the record. In a 2020 design draft, Brian Goetz pointed out that while a class has O(n) getters, it "could conceivably have O(2^n) withers", and asked that hand-written withers not become a best practice. Write withers only for the changes your domain actually makes.

A language fix exists on paper. JEP 468, derived record creation, proposes refund with { amountMinor = 2_000; }. It would take the record apart, run the block, and call the canonical constructor with the result. It is a Candidate JEP, no JDK has shipped it, and in January 2026 Goetz wrote that it "has been 'on hold' for a while". Don't plan around it.

The other differences matter more day to day. A data class may declare properties in its body, and Kotlin leaves those out of equals, hashCode, toString and copy(), so two objects that differ only there are equal. A record can't have body state at all. A data class can't be open, abstract or sealed, and a record is always final. Kotlin destructures with val (id, amount) = refund, through componentN() functions, while Java destructures with record patterns in switch and instanceof (lesson 3).

Where the two languages meet, Kotlin reads a Java record's accessors as properties (money.minor), and @JvmRecord on a data class emits a real java.lang.Record that Java code sees as one. The Kotlin docs warn that adding @JvmRecord to an existing class is not a binary-compatible change, so decide when you create the class.

try.title: Wither versus copy()
steps: Run WitherDemo and its twin WitherDemoKt. Compare the four lines each prints.
Add a withPaymentId(String id) wither to the Java record and call it with " ". Should that be rejected? Add the check where every wither will get it.
In WitherDemo.kt, add var note = "" to the body of RefundRequest, set full.note = "called twice", and print full == full.copy() and full.copy().note.

code.title: WitherDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo; import java.util.List; /** Java has no copy(): you write withers by hand, and each one calls the canonical constructor. */ public class WitherDemo { record Refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor, List<String> reasons) { Refund { if (amountMinor <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("refund must be positive: " + amountMinor); reasons = List.copyOf(reasons); } Refund withAmount(long newAmount) { return new Refund(paymentId, newAmount, reasons); } Refund withReason(String extra) { var more = new java.util.ArrayList<>(reasons); more.add(extra); return new Refund(paymentId, amountMinor, more); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Refund full = new Refund("pay_81", 5_000, List.of("duplicate charge")); Refund part = full.withAmount(2_000).withReason("partial goodwill"); System.out.println("original: " + full); System.out.println("changed: " + part); System.out.println("same reasons list object: " + (full.reasons() == full.withAmount(1_000).reasons())); try { full.withAmount(-1); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("wither ran the checks: " + e.getMessage()); } } }

alt.title: WitherDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo // Kotlin generates copy(): one "wither" with a named, defaulted parameter per property data class RefundRequest(val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long, val reasons: List<String>) { init { require(amountMinor > 0) { "refund must be positive: $amountMinor" } } } /** copy() runs init, and like a Java wither it copies references, not what they point to. */ fun main() { val full = RefundRequest("pay_81", 5_000, listOf("duplicate charge")) val part = full.copy(amountMinor = 2_000, reasons = full.reasons + "partial goodwill") println("original: $full") println("changed: $part") println("same reasons list object: ${full.reasons === full.copy(amountMinor = 1_000).reasons}") try { full.copy(amountMinor = -1) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("copy ran the checks: ${e.message}") } }

try.expect: Both versions print the original, the changed refund, same reasons list object: true and a rejected negative amount. Withers and copy() both reuse the component references, which is safe here only because the list can't change. The blank-id check belongs in the compact constructor, so every wither inherits it. In Kotlin, full == full.copy() is true and the copy's note is empty: body properties are ignored by equals and not copied.

analogy: A record is like a line on a printed bank statement: date, amount, reference. Anyone can read every field, two lines with the same values mean the same thing, and to change one you print a new line. The bank checks the line before it prints it, which is the compact constructor's job. The analogy breaks at one point: a printed line can't point at anything that changes later, while a record's List component can be someone else's list that keeps growing after the record was made.
world: Your Quarkus services already move records around: REST request and response bodies, Kafka event payloads, Temporal activity inputs. Each of those is a boundary where outside data becomes a value, and the compact constructor is where you check it once: three-letter currency codes, non-negative amounts, idempotency keys of the right length. After that, any Money the service holds is a valid one. Two places need care. A List component in a Kafka event must be copied, or a producer that reuses its buffer list changes events it has already handed off. And a record that holds a PAN, an IBAN or an access token must override toString, because the generated one prints every component into every log line and exception message that touches the record.
mistake: The common mistake is treating a record as deeply immutable and using it as a map or set key while one of its components is a mutable list or map. It works in tests, because nothing mutates the list there. In production a caller reuses its ArrayList, the record's hashCode changes, and HashMap.get returns null for a key that is still in the map. Copy every collection component in the compact constructor with List.copyOf, Set.copyOf or Map.copyOf, and don't use arrays as components.

compare.title: A validated money value in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Money.java
java.html: public record Money(long minor, String currency) { private static final Pattern ISO = Pattern.compile("[A-Z]{3}"); public Money { Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency"); currency = currency.trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT); // normalize in place if (!ISO.matcher(currency).matches()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad currency: " + currency); if (minor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount: " + minor); } public Money plus(Money other) { if (!currency.equals(other.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch"); return new Money(Math.addExact(minor, other.minor), currency); } }

kotlin.title: Money.kt
kotlin.html: data class Money(val minor: Long, val currency: String) { init { require(ISO.matches(currency)) { "bad currency: $currency" } // can reject, can't normalize require(minor >= 0) { "negative amount: $minor" } } operator fun plus(other: Money): Money { require(currency == other.currency) { "currency mismatch" } return Money(Math.addExact(minor, other.minor), currency) } companion object { private val ISO = Regex("[A-Z]{3}") fun of(minor: Long, currency: String) = Money(minor, currency.trim().uppercase()) } }

compare.note: Both give you equals, hashCode and toString over all components, final fields, and a validation hook that every construction goes through, including Kotlin's copy(). Three things differ. Java's compact constructor can normalize a parameter before it becomes a field; a data class can only reject it, so normalizing lives in a factory and the public constructor stays open to raw input. Java deserialization rebuilds a record through its canonical constructor but skips a data class's init (@JvmRecord closes that gap). And Kotlin has copy() with named arguments, while Java has hand-written withers until JEP 468 ships, which it hasn't.

worked.title: Turn a mutable request class into a record

steps.say: A capture request in a payment service is a JavaBean: setters, a mutable list, and sixty lines of hand-written equals, hashCode and toString that nobody updated when currency was added. Any code can change it after it was checked.
steps.code: public class CaptureRequest { private String paymentId; private long amountMinor; private String currency; private List<String> lineItems = new ArrayList<>(); public void setAmountMinor(long amountMinor) { this.amountMinor = amountMinor; } public List<String> getLineItems() { return lineItems; } // hands out the live list // ... more setters, getters, equals, hashCode, toString }

alt.html: class CaptureRequest { var paymentId: String? = null var amountMinor: Long = 0 var currency: String? = null val lineItems: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf() // hands out the live list }

steps.say: Write the header. The components are the whole state, and every setter is gone. Recompile: each place that called a setter is now a compile error, which is your list of code that mutated a request after it was built.
steps.code: // 1. the components are the state public record CaptureRequest(String paymentId, Money amount, List<String> lineItems) {}

alt.html: // 1. the properties are the state data class CaptureRequest(val paymentId: String, val amount: Money, val lineItems: List<String>)

steps.say: Add the compact constructor. Reject what can't be valid, then copy the list so the caller can't change it later. amount is a Money, which validates itself, so the request doesn't repeat those checks.
steps.code: public record CaptureRequest(String paymentId, Money amount, List<String> lineItems) { public CaptureRequest { Objects.requireNonNull(paymentId, "paymentId"); // 2. reject Objects.requireNonNull(amount, "amount"); if (paymentId.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("blank paymentId"); lineItems = List.copyOf(lineItems); // 3. copy if (lineItems.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no line items"); } }

alt.html: data class CaptureRequest(val paymentId: String, val amount: Money, val lineItems: List<String>) { init { require(paymentId.isNotBlank()) { "blank paymentId" } // 2. reject require(lineItems.isNotEmpty()) { "no line items" } } companion object { fun of(paymentId: String, amount: Money, lineItems: List<String>) = CaptureRequest(paymentId, amount, java.util.List.copyOf(lineItems)) // 3. copy } }

steps.say: Add only the wither the domain needs. Partial captures happen, so withAmount earns its place. It calls the canonical constructor, so a partial capture can't skip the checks. In Kotlin, copy(amount = ...) already exists and runs init.
steps.code: // 4. one wither, through the canonical constructor public CaptureRequest withAmount(Money partial) { return new CaptureRequest(paymentId, partial, lineItems); }

alt.html: // 4. no wither to write: copy() is generated and runs init val partial = request.copy(amount = Money.of(2_000, "eur"))

lab.title: Payment value records
steps: Run the tests once. All eight fail. Read the test names in PaymentRecordsTest: they are the spec.
In Money, write the compact constructor (TODO 1) and plus (TODO 2).
In Refund, write the compact constructor with a defensive copy of the reasons (TODO 3), then withAmount (TODO 4).

Order matters in Money: normalize first, then check for three letters, or " eur " fails the check.
List.copyOf(reasons) throws NullPointerException for a null list, so it does that null check for you.

drill.title: A validated key from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write record IdempotencyKey(String value) that rejects null, trims the value, and then rejects anything that isn't 16 to 64 letters, digits or -. Then write the Kotlin version. Which of the two can store the trimmed value without a factory?

answer.html: public record IdempotencyKey(String value) { private static final Pattern SHAPE = Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9-]{16,64}"); public IdempotencyKey { Objects.requireNonNull(value, "value"); value = value.trim(); // normalize first if (!SHAPE.matcher(value).matches()) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad idempotency key"); } } }

alt.html: data class IdempotencyKey(val value: String) { init { require(SHAPE.matches(value)) { "bad idempotency key" } // can reject, can't trim } companion object { private val SHAPE = Regex("[A-Za-z0-9-]{16,64}") fun of(raw: String) = IdempotencyKey(raw.trim()) // so trimming lives here } }

recap: A record is a final class with private final fields, public accessors, one canonical constructor and generated equals, hashCode and toString. It can't add instance fields or extend a class.
Validate and normalize in the compact constructor. Every path goes through it: new, factories, other constructors, withers and Java deserialization.
Equality compares every component: Objects.equals for references and compare for primitives, so NaN equals NaN and 0.0 doesn't equal -0.0. Arrays compare by reference.
Records are only shallowly immutable. Copy collection components with List.copyOf, or a mutated key gets lost in a HashSet.
The generated methods read fields, not accessors. To hide a secret, override toString.
Kotlin has copy() and Java has hand-written withers, because JEP 468 is on hold. Java deserialization skips a data class's init unless the class is @JvmRecord.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Our Payout(String iban, long amount, List<String> tags) record is immutable, so it's safe to keep in a HashSet and to log as it is." Explain, in your own words, the two ways that can go wrong and what you would change.
explain.answer: A record is only shallowly immutable. Its fields can't be reassigned, but tags points to whatever list the caller passed, and if the caller keeps changing that list the record's hashCode changes and the set can't find it any more. Copy the list in the compact constructor with List.copyOf. Logging is the second problem: the generated toString prints every component, so the full IBAN goes into the logs. Overriding the iban() accessor doesn't help, because toString reads the field directly. Override toString and print a masked IBAN there.

deeper.html:
Two details round out the picture.

A Java record can't hide its canonical constructor. The Record Javadoc says it "must provide at least as much access as the record class", and javac enforces it:

Java
public record Key(String v) { private Key { } }
// error: invalid canonical constructor in record Key
//   (attempting to assign stronger access privileges; was public)
Kotlin
data class Key private constructor(val v: String) {
    companion object { fun of(raw: String) = Key(raw.trim()) }
}
// warning (Kotlin 2.4): non-public primary constructor is exposed via the generated 'copy()' method

So validation must live inside the constructor, where nobody can bypass it. Kotlin lets you make a data class constructor private and force callers through a factory that normalizes, but copy() still exposes it. Kotlin 2.4.21 warns about this, says the warning becomes an error in language version 2.5, and offers @ConsistentCopyVisibility to make copy() as private as the constructor.

The second detail is about what comes after records. In a January 2026 design note, "Data-Oriented Programming for Java: Beyond Records", Brian Goetz describes the cliff you fall off when a class is almost a record: one derived field or one private cache, and you are back to writing everything by hand. The note sketches carrier classes, written like class Point(int x, int y) { ... }: a normal class with a record-style state description. The language would require the canonical constructor and the accessors and give the class a deconstruction pattern, while the class declares its own fields and need not be final. It is a design note, not a JEP, so treat it as a direction, not a feature.

sources.title: Brian Goetz, Data Classes and Sealed Types for Java (2019)
